House in committee on Bill (No. 195), respecting the currency.-Mr. Fielding.
On section 12, no other coins to be legal tender.

I would again urge the minister to change the five-cent coins, because it is a universal complaint that the five-cent piece we have is so small that it is easily lost, and whilst it is a very nice coin it would be a far greater convenience if we employed base metal and adopted some system such as they have in other countries for that class of coin. I also think the one-cent piece contains far too much metal. There is no intention on the part of the government to say that the copper contained in it bears any relation to the value of the coin, and it is exactly the same size as a 25 cent piece, so that it is difficult to distinguish them. Each denomination should be of a different size, so that the coins can be distinguished by touch. Every one has been looking forward to a change when the minister was revising the Currency Act, and I think public opinion is strongly in favour of such a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not heard much evidence of a general desire to make these changes, and I must confess that I have in some respects what I may describe as a wholesome conservatism and' adherence to old established things. My hon. friend's touch is not as keen as it used to be; I have put the 25 cent piece and the cent together and they are not the same size.
Mr. SPROULE I have been spoken to in respect to this once or twice in view of the expected changes, and my experience is the reverse of the hon. member for
North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie). I would doubt the wisdom of making any change from the coins we are familiar with.
I do not know of any country with such a small silver coin as ours. The Americans abolished it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have in England a three-penny piece about the same size.

It is a very rare coin.
On section 21, appointment of assay commissioners, examination, and test, &c.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In England they have what is called the trial of the Pyx which takes place at Goldsmith's Hall, and they utilize for this purpose the services of the Goldsmith's Company. This is a trial to test the correctness of the coin. We have not in Canada a corresponding organization, and we propose once a year to appoint three gentlemen who shall test the coin, and guarantee to the public that it is of correct weight and quality. It follows in substance the English practice, but the method is different, because we have not the same organization here.
To whom do they report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the Governor in Council, and I suppose like any other public document it would be brought before parliament.
What is to be their remuneration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The compensation for this service in England takes the shape of a public dinner at Goldsmith's Hall, but we have not yet determined the compensation to be paid to the gentlemen in Canada.	i
Give them a dinner at the parliamentary restaurant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That might do.
Is not the test made in the presence of the officials of the House of Commons, and the House of Lords, is it not rather a state function in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is the dinner that is the state function.
On section 22, Dominion standard Troy ounce to be standard of weight, weights to be verified and approved.

Where is this standard Troy ounce to be checked or verified? In Great Britain? I understand that the American standard Troy weight has recently been tested and found a little off. Will our test be in Goldsmith's Hall in England. 1 or what is t-o be the standard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) is nof present, and -so I cannot offer any explanation further than that we refer to the standard weights of the Inland Revenue Department as established by the Weights and Measures Act.

But would the standard weights of the Inland Revenue Department, such as are used ordinarily throughout the country, be sufficient for the purposes of the Finance Department? I should think that the standards in this matter should be under control of the Finance Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue has these standards for all purposes, and we simply declare the standards thus established shall be accepted for the purposes of our department.
And where is this Troy weight fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can only say that it is fixed by the Weights and Measures Act. Further than that, I cannot answer.
On the schedule,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I want to make an addition to the schedule to correspond with the decision already reached by the committee respecting the creation of the silver dollar. In the schedule as it is at present, there is no reference to that point, and, as the silver dollar is to be made, it must be provided for in the schedule, like the rest. The amendment I propose is to insert in the schedule the following:
Under denomination of coin-silver ; one dollar, standard weight 360 grains; remedy allowance-weight per piece; 1-50 grains; mil-lesitnal fineness, 4.
May I ask the Minister of Finance why it is he wants to coin a silver dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have already had quite a discussion on that point. In brief, representations were made to me by hon members from British Columbia both in this House and in the Senate, that the creation of a silver dollar was very desirable from a British Columbia point of view, and I have found by experience that there is a taste for the American silver dollar on the Pacific side. I see no reason why, there being a demand, we should not supply it, rather than use the American dollar. If our dollar note is not sufficient, and there are people who want a silver dollar, I think it is good business to furnish it.

I would suggest to the minister the coining of the Mexican dollar, as it is called, with a view to enable Canada to export silver to China, Japan Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
and other eastern countries. Hong Kong or Mexican dollar is the standard in silver countries. And, as we hope to take a prominent place in the trade of the Orient, if we are to have a silver dollar, I think we should have a coin that will be of use in that trade. We are large producers of silver, and these eastern countries will furnish a great market. I think it would be much better to make a coin of the exchange value of the Hong Kong or Mexican dollar than one that would be useful in exchange only in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not much enamoured of the silver dollar. At present we want to confine ourselves to the use of it in Canada. The other question that the hon. member has raised is a much larger one and one upon which I would not care to enter at present.

I do not wish to take up time if this matter is already decided. But I may remind the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that in the United States silver dollars are piled up unused- they cannot circulate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure niv hon.
friend (Mr. Perley) that the law of supply and demand will govern that. We have no desire to coin them unless there is a demand for them, and I realize that that demand may arise only on the Pacific coast.

Perhaps the information I am about to ask has already been given. I would like to know what profits the government made last year from the mint, and how these profits compare with what we should have made if we had not had a mint. It is mainly on the silver coins, I believe, that we make a profit in the minting operations. Formerly, we had an arrangement with the imperial authorities that they were to coin for us. Had we not changed that and established a mint here, what would have been the difference in our profits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The information asked for has not been given to-day. But a return was brought down some time ago, and will be found in the records, which, I think, covers the whole matter. In general terms, the position is this : while there is a large profit in the operation of the mint, it is undoubtedly a fact that if we were content to have our coins made as in former years, in England, we should make a larger profit. That I state unhesitatingly. But, on the same principle, no doubt, we could get our Dominion notes printed more cheaply in England than here, yet it was thought that there were good reasons why we should have an establishment for that purpose in Ottawa. The same reasons extended to coinage lead us to think it is better to have Canadian

coins made in Canada. The making of them is profitable, not as regards gold- there is no profit in coining gold-but in the silver coins and bronze coins. But, as a mere matter of profits, we should do better by having our coins made in England.

CL'RRIE. The current impression is that the coins of this country were formerly minted at the royal mint in England Is it not a fact, however, that many of these were coined by British contractors . in Birmingham and other places who make coins for other countries, and not in the royal mint?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our orders were invariably sent to the royal mint. But in several instances, because the royal mint was too busy or for some other reason, they turned our orders over to contractors in Birmingham. So, in that sense, the hon. member's statement is practically correct.
Has the hon. minister considered any design for the gold coins?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The design is not finally adopted. It is being prepared in the royal mint in England! The elements will be, first, the King's head, as a matter of course, and the arms of Canada, will be used as the chief features in the design. These, with the designation of the coin, the word 'Canada', and the date are the elements of which the design is being made up.

It is necessary that we should have some name for the $5 gold piece, and the design has a good deal to do with the name. Every country has a special name for its ordinary gold piece, and we should have some short- name.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What do you call the sovereign?

I call it a sovereign. It is called a napoleon in France, an eagle in the United States, a crown in some parts of Europe, and there must be a short name for the $5 gold piece in Canada, for instance, the beaver.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The design at present proposed is the King's head and the arms of Canada. While the beaver has elements of value as an industrious animal, I am not quite sure that it is a thing of beauty.
The minister may be sure that the general public will give a name of its own to the new gold piece, and he might keep that in mind when forming the design, if he does not like the beaver.

CL'RRIE. Is it the intention to follow the new American practice in the
die? The old American coinage is always in relief. They have reversed that in the new coin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe it was found that the American gold piece, while beautiful in its design, would not stack, and for certain purposes that was a defect in the American currency.
When the minister speaks of the arms of Canada, does he mean the arms of Canada before confederation, or does he mean the arms of the Dominion as they now exist?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a matter of so much importance as a coin, we would have to use the authorized arms, and for the present we would not include a representation of all the provinces. But no doubt before long we will have to have a new issue in which the new arms will be used. For the 'present we only take the authorized arms.

I would suggest to the minister that a wheat sheaf on the gold coin would be a good advertisement for the country.

Before you leave the Chair, I desire to call the attention of the Alinister of Finance to a matter of considerable importance affecting the gardeners of Alanitoba, and I presume of all Canada. I am in receipt of a letter from the reeve of the municipality of Kildonan. in my county, who is also the secretary of the Agricultural Society of that municipality. He writes as follows:
You will notice by the papers that the wholesalers of the west have petitioned the government to remove the duty from fruit and green vegetables coming into Canada between December 1 and July 31. Our gardeners protest against the time being extended past June 15, as our stock grown here is in by that time. If this goes into force it will put a lot of our gardeners out of business. We are sending a small petition against it to the government to-day. As the time is short we cannot wait to go to everybody. AYe want you, when it comes up, to do what you can for us, and we think the 15th of June should be the latest. Will inclose article out of paper.
I have the inclosed petition here, which I presume the minister has received from the wholesalers of the wrest, and I will read a part of it. It is addressed to His Excellency, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, making, as you will see, a little mistake at the beginning :

Sir,-Your petitioners represent the principal fruit and vegetable importing concerns in western Canada.
Little fruit is raised in western Canada, and the western cities are dependent upon the United States for all the earlv fruit and vegetables. These come from as far south as Miami, Florida. During the several months of the year before it is possible to grow vegetables or fruits, a large quantity of both are imported; but the freight charges coupled with the duty, place the consumption beyond the purse of the average householder, and these products become a luxury when they are really a necessity.
Our desire is-and we believe it to be a reflex of that of the western country at large- that the duty be removed from these products at such times when they cannot possibly come into competition with home grown articles. YVe believe that the adoption of the following schedule would be of distinct advantage, supplying the people of western Canada with some of the necessities of life which the country, by reason of its geographical position, is not able to provide at those times.
Schedule.
Peaches, pears, plums and apricots on free list from January 1 to October 1.
Cherries, on free list from January 1 to June 30.	[DOT]
Grapes, on free list from December 1 to August 31.
Tomatoes, and green vegetables, cabbage, cucumbers, celery, asparagus, rhubarb, green bea,ns, cauliflower, on free list from December 1 to July 31.
_ It is this last paragraph, Mr. Speaker, in which I am most interested, because it affects the great garden industry in our part of the country. I may say that two-thirds of the gardens in the west are situated in my own county. The gardeners have a large amount of money invested in this industry, and while the wholesalers are petitioning apparently in the interest of the consumer, I have grave doubts, if their petition was acceded to, that the general consumer would benefit very much. You simply place in the hands of the wholesaler a power to force the gardeners of our own country to sell to the wholesalers at a reduced price when their stuff comes into the market. I want to protest strongly against the government acceding to the request of the wholesaler as regards the admission of tomatoes, green vegetables, cabbage, cucumbers, asparagus, rhubarb, green beans and cauliflower being placed on the free list from December 1, to July 31. The gardeners seem to be quite willing that they should be placed on the free list, but not later than the 15th of June, and plied with these articles by our own gardeners. All the way from Winnipeg down to Selkirk the gardeners have established a very large business. The gardener really makes his profit on the early vegetables, and the wholesalers apparently want the duty removed so that American stuff may be brought into competition with our garden Mr. BRADBURY.
stuff just at the time when there is any money in it for the gardner. I appeal to the minister on behalf of the gardeners of Manitoba and, I presume, the whole of Canada that they shall receive fair protection against any foreign importation of vegetables. Last year the question was broached by some of the gardeners about asking the government to put an increased protection on some of these vegetables that come from the other side-cabbage and such like-and I hope the government will take this into their serious consideration and see that the [DOT] American producer is not allowed to interfere with the gardeners of this country.

I am quite persuaded that the minister or the government would not accede to or deal with a proposition of that kind lightly. We are aware of that and certainly I would utter a very strong protest if a matter of that kind were dealt with without the fullest consideration of the other side of the question. As a matter of fact a disturbance of the duties referred to by my hon. friend would interfere decidedly with the enormous acreage of fruit in our own province of British Columbia where we are building up .a tremendous industry and considering that the whole schedule of the American tariff is against us so strongly that we cannot send any of these commodities into the United States it is quite palpable that we could not, without the strongest protest, have such a recommendation as that listened to without the fullest consideration.

My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) says that he represents two-thirds of the market gardeners of Manitoba. He may have something that will support that statement but I represent a constituency that comes up close to the city of Winnipeg, and I think that possibly there are as many market gardeners in the constituency of Macdonald as there are in Selkirk. Therefore, I want to endorse what my hon. friend from Selkirk has said on behalf of the market gardeners of my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have received, within a few days, a copy of a petition dealing with the condition explained to the House by the hon. member for Selkirk. The petition was from the importers. It was followed somewhat rapidly by a communication from the fruit growers of the Niagara district protesting in the strongest terms against what was proposed by the importers of Winnipeg, and now we have the additional protest of the hon. gentleman. What has been said to-day indicates clearly that it is a much disputed matter, to which there are certainly two sides, and I can assure my hon. friends that at this stage of the session we would not undertake to make any disturbance of the tariff

on that matter. What has been said wil. be a fair matter for inquiry and for any future action, but nothing will be done at. the present session.

If the Minister of Finance is going to listen only to the views of the importers of this country the rest of the people might as well close up shop and go out of business. The importers are interested in importations and not in the local or native industries, and the minister on these matters apparently is prepared to give the importers a more attentive ear than the poor man who is trying to make a living. The chief grievance of these fruit growers of the Niagara district applies to all the growers of small fruits and the market gardeners of this country. These men of Canada are just as much entitled to justice as are the importers of Winnipeg or any other city who are endeavouring to make a big lot of money out of importing foreign fruit in cold storage. This is a matter of placing the handling of all our vegetables and fruits in the hands of the cold storage trusts, and I think we should stand by our own people on a question of this kind and not in favour of the importers as the minister does.

I would like to add a word or two on behalf of the market gardeners of my county and to urge that no action may be taken without an opportunity oi being given the gardeners of that section to lay their case before the government. I am quite sure that no action will be taken. I desire to say just one thing further and that is that the people of Canada must bear in mind that the market gardeners are producing many things now that we never thought would be produced in Canada many years ago. They are producing large quantities of products now that heretofore were imported from the United States. Within this very year, in my own time, some men have given up their ordinary avocations, have taken up pieces oi land and are going especially into the market gardening business for the purpose of raising early products which are used in our houses and have a large sale in the early part of the year. Therefore, I would ask that the government, in the consideration of the tariff question as it affects the farmers and market gardeners of this country, would keep in mind the fact that both farmers and market gardeners are able to produce a great many things to-day that in years back they could not produce at all, and I am quite sure that so long as matters are left steadfast they will produce everything at almost any time of the year that the people of this country will require.

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance when we may
expect the information which was asked for with respect to the' proposed changes in the tariff?

Civil government-Post Office Department- salaries, $546,260.
Does the Postmaster General intend to increase the salaries of the railway mail clerks, and if not, why not?

That question was put by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Mac-dpnell) yesterday, and my answer appears in ' Hansard/ Last year I gave a general increase to the lower classes of the outside service, sorters, stampers and labourers, and this year I thought we should give an increase to the higher classes, who had not received .any increase since confederation. Some years ago the railway mail clerks received a substantial increase, and as there is a general demand for higher salaries on the part of the city office sorters and clerks, the question arises whether we should increase the one and not the others. I have decided, after the session, to examine the various merits or demerits of the claims put forth, and at the beginning of next session, I hope to be able to introduce legislation on the matter. My intention is to bring the outside service in the larger city post offices under the Civil Service Act. We can do so under an order in council, but pre-' liminary to that we have to adjust the salaries so that the different classes of employees may fall into a proper salary classification.
Is the minister in a position to state now that he will bring the outside post office service under the Civil Service Act and rearrange the salaries?
Speaking for myself personally, it is my intention to do so. The department is studying the problem, which is a very difficult one.

What action has the minister taken in regard to the application for a post office at Kilmant and Shacleton, which are situated outside of Winnipeg? In 1906, this post office was recommended by Mr. Riddel, who being the defeated candidate, apparently had the patronage, and every year since the minister has -had it brought to his notice. Last year the minister assured me that he was going to give the people of that district a post office, and that it would not be necessary for me to bring the matter up in the House. A post office is certainly required in that locality. There are no post offices, from Winnipeg west about 15 miles, on the south side of the river, and while there are post

offices on the other side of the river at certain seasons of the year, the people cannot cross and cannot get their mail unless they go through the city of Winnipeg, a distance of 8 miles. A. return which has been brought down, gives the correspondence addressed to the minister as to the necessity for this post office. The whole trouble has been over some little political disappointment, and the person who had the patronage of that constituency advised that there should not be a post office there. There is no doubt in my mind; there cannot be any cloubt in the mind of the minister if he has read the correspondence, that there is great necessity for a post office at that point. Is the minister going to give the people of this locality a post office, which they have so long been asking for? Might I also ask, now that Dr. Thompson, the defeated candidate, is dead, who has the patronage of that locality? As the defeated candidate has passed to his reward, might I, as the representative of that constituency, have a little to say in the distribution of the patronage and towards securing what the people really require?

I should have informed my hon. friend about a fortnight ago, that a report had been sent to me by Post Office Inspector McLeod, of Winnipeg, which I have approved. At the request of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) I asked for a special report as to the necessity of the office referred to, and the inspector recommended the opening of an office, which, I think, is at Kilmant Park, but I do not know that the office has been opened under that name, but from Mr. McLeod's report, the new office, which has been opened, will serve the hon. gentleman's purpose, and especially serve the needs of the patrons in that neighbourhood. We have closed one office on the other side of the river, and by equalizing the distances between the neighbouring offices, according to Mr. McLeod, we are giving satisfaction to the patrons concerned. If the office has not been opened, it will be in a day or so.
I have had no advice that the office is opened, but I am pleased to know that the minister has given instructions that it should be opened.

As regards the patronage,
I know that Mr. Thompson, who was the Liberal candidate, is dead, as we generally do in all these matters, we referred the question to the inspector. Of course, when a postmaster is to be appointed we generally ask our political friends, we are human enough for that, but as to the location of a post office or its necessity we take the advice of the post office inspector.
Has mv hon. friend also a patronage list?	'

I do not know of any in the department. My hon. friend himself *asked me last year to open an office which he thought was necessary in his constituency. I looked into the case,, got a report, and opened the office at his request.

Perhaps he is on the list.
.Mr. BLAIN. I appreciate very much the kindness of the department and" the minister in opening an office in my county, and I may say that lids friends as well as my own appreciate that very much. It would not be open to criticism from any class of people, it is meeting the wants of the people,. and I am sure the opening of that office will stand to the credit of the government. I suppose my hon. friend does not put any advertisements in newspapers?
Yes, I think we do.
How .is that list?

I could not give it offhand. We could not have a patronage list, properly speaking, for the very reason that according to law I am obliged to advertise in each case when there is a new mail contract to be awarded, if it is for more than $200, unless when a contract has been going on for some years to the satisfaction of the department and a renewal is to the interest of the department. I could not give a list of the papers in which the advertisements appear because that is done through the Department of the Secretary of State.
Does my hon. friend lay down a principle that where a paper has the largest circulation in a district, advertisements should be inserted in it regardless of its politics
He advertises by posters.
Oh, no; he inserts these advertisements in the newspapers as well.

Very little, we advertise very little; as the hon. gentleman from Grey pointed out our advertisements are placarded in every post office and country store and in Quebec at the church doors. I may say that if perchance there is an advertisement to be inserted I am human enough to give the preference to a good Grit paper.
Why?

Because I am a man and not an angel. I must say, however, that the absence of a Grit paper would necessitate the advertisement being put in a good Tory paper, and that has happened on more than one occasion.

I am referring to advertisements calling for tenders for the renewal of contracts or for new contracts. I can

produce Reform newspapers from my own county containing advertisements calling for tenders to be sent in to the department. When my hon. friend states that the custom is to print a circular and post it up in the post offices, and that is the sum total of the advertisements, I hardly think he will venture to say that it is the government policy.
That is generally what we do.
It would be interesting to have a list of the Conservative newspapers in which he has inserted Advertisements in the past year.

I have two in my mind just now. In the northern section of the Ottawa district, some new contracts were awarded to change the service from biweekly to tri-weekly, and from tri-weekly to daily. There are only two papers in that district, one English, and one French, and both Conservative-the Pontiac ' Advance ' and ' Le Pionier de Nominingue '. I did not know that these papers were in existence, I have not time to read them, but my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Major) stated very frankly that there were no other papers in that district, and advised me to send the advertisements to these two. Here are two Conservative papers to which I sent advertisements. The list is not very long, and I mention these from memory."

That is a very frank admission and I may congratulate the hon. minister on his list. It is larger than that of the Department of Public Works, which was handed across the House the other evening, and which was blank. My hon. friend required to advertise, and finding there were no Reform newspapers in that locality, he gave the advertisements to the only two papers published there. That is a little better than the record of the Minister of Public Works, and therefore, I offer the hon. gentleman my congratulations.
The district is a large one, sparsely and wildly settled.
I would like to know who the postmaster is to be.
There are two St. Charles, and I am afraid to confuse the two. One was abolished to make way for the other. If my hon. friend will put a question on the order paper, I will give him the information.
Did you call for tenders?
If the service is opened, we must have. If my hon. friend will put a question on the order paper, I will give him an answer.
The minister cannot give information as to whether he called for tenders or not, but simply states that he is going to establish a post office there.
We may not have called for tenders if it is the extension of an existing contract. In that case the contractor takes the new contract at a pro rata rate.

The people of that district have been suffering for the want of a post office. They had the promise of the minister a year ago, and now he tells us he is going to give that post office. I presume, therefore, that beyond doubt there will be a post office established immediately in that district.

I have not the papers under my hand just now, but I can assure my hon. friend that not later than two or three weeks ago I approved a report signed by Mr. McLeod, of Winnipeg, our inspector, in favour of the establishment of a post office such as was requested by my hon. friend at the end of last session, and I know that we decided to dispense with one of the St. Charles post offices. Thera were two post offices, and there was a quarrel on that side of the river as to the location. Following the suggestion made by the inspector, I dispensed with one of these and equalized the distance between the two, so as to give the people the office they wanted.

Then we may take it for granted that beyond doubt that post office will be established immediately. I would like to ask the minister what action he has taken in response to the petition I sent him a short time ago from the citizens of Rose-dale asking that a daily mail be established in that district. The present service is largely temporary, and has only been triweekly, or possibly twice a week for Lev-ingham. The minister has that petition in his hands at present. The people are. anxious to have a daily mail service put on that branch line.
I will see that my hon. friend is satisfied.

I do not know that I want to oppose the necessary increases to salaries, but inasmuch as the hon. the Postmaster General has said that he accepts the reports of his inspectors of districts, as to whether or not a post office should be granted, or a more frequent service, I must assume that with regard to the petition which I presented to him asking for a better mail service in the county of Fron-tenac, he was influenced in his decision by the report of the inspector of that district. If I am right in that conclusion, the sooner he gets a new inspector for the district the better for the people. I want to point out to him that in my judgment his department is giving more attention to the mail service in the cities and large cen-
What do you estimate as the additional cost?

The cost of a daily instead of a tri-weekly service to Latimer will be less than the department has been paying if you take into consideration the fact that you are going to get the mail carried for less this year than last, because of the fact that the mail contractor in tendering for the contract lowered his price $50 because of the abolition of tolls on the-road. But I want to direct attention strongly to the point that the Latimer post office, with a tri-weekly service, is giving a revenue of $74.25 a year, and I think it reasonable to conclude that if they had a daily service the revenue would be increased, a little at all events. I know whereof I speak when I say that you can get the mail carried from the stage to the Latimer post office for $90, the same as you are paying for carrying the mail from the stage to Glen-burnie post office. You have only a difference of $15.75, if we assume that you would have no increased revenue from a daily service over a tri-weekly service.
Now, I want to call attention to another post office. The Postmaster General, in answering a letter of mine in regard to the Latimer post office, said that he was of the opinion that, even with the limited amount of post office business transacted, the triweekly service was reasonable. Now, I say again that if he bases that opinion- I know he cannot keep in touch with every office-if he bases that opinion on any report sent by the inspector of the Kingston district, then the sooner he gets a new inspector the better for the department and for the people in general.
I want to call his attention to another case in my county, the case of the Wil-liamsville post office. A great many years ago, before letter-carriers were appointed in the city of Kingston, Williamsville was within the city limits and was made a post office. It was supposed that Williamsville would supply the people of the upper end of the city as well as the people in the county adjoining. Since then, letter-carriers have been appointed to carry the mails to the people in the city of Kingston, and they even carry the mail to the postmaster who keeps the Williamsville post office.
I have asked that the Williamsville post office be moved up the street about three-quarters of a mile to the border of the city with the county. Now, that seems to me to be reasonable. It would be about 150 yards away from the school house, and the change would not cost 'one cent, because the same stage which drops the mail off at the Williamsville post office, the Kingston and Newburgh stage, would pass up the street and drop it off at a store in the upper part of the city. Look at the advantage it would be to the people. Children going to school in the morning could post their letters, and after school at night they could call at the post office and get their mail before going home. It would be a great convenience to the people of the surrounding country in that vicinity, and petition after petition has been sent here by the people of that section asking for this to be done. Would it be any detriment to the people of the city of Kingston? Not one particle of detriment, because the letter-carriers in the city take the letters right past the Williamsville post office and all around through th'at part of the city, and three-quarters of a mile up the street to the boundary between the city and the county. Why should that not be done? I did not ask, and do not ask now, to move the post office out into the county. I am willing that the member for the city of Kingston should have the privilege of saying wffiere the post office should be established, and of naming a person living in the city to keep the post office. But I repeat that it does seem to me extremely unfair to the people in that section of the country that they should be deprived of a better mail service when they could get it without doing any harm or causing any inconvenience whatever to the people of the upper part of the city.
I want to call attention to another request which I made for a post office. I asked the deputy minister to establish a post office midway between Maberley and Sharbot Lake, at a place called Fall River. A largely signed petition was sent down here asking for that convenience. The nearest any person in that locality is to a post office is four and a half miles, they have to go from four to seven miles in . order to get their mail. They asked for a mail twice a week only. There is a cheese factory and quite a settlement, and they only ask for a mail twice a week. What is the answer?	That it
would cost $70 a year to take the mail

in there, and that the postmaster's salary would be $35 a year, that is $105, and that the revenue would possibly be no more than. $10.
To carry the mail between what two points?

The minister's letter stated that the location would be about four miles and a half from Maberley, but it does not lie in a direct line between Sharbot Lake and1 Maberley. If you take the point where they want a post office established as one point, and Sharbot Lake as another, and Maberley as another, they would form a triangle, so you cannot * exactly say that the point where they want the post office is midway between Sharbot Lake and Maberley. Now, 1 am sorry the minister takes the view that, because this office would only accommodate, as he says in his letter, some twenty families, he cannot afford to expend that amount of money per year in the county of Frontenac and give those people a mail service twice a week. I want to express my view very strongly that the Postmaster General has no right to one dollar of surplus in his department. The money that he gets in his department comes from the postage stamps and post cards purchased by the people, and that money should go' back to the people in the way of mail service. I think it speaks very poorly indeed for the Post Office Department if they cannot afford to expend in that county a small amount like that.
Now, I want to add to what I have said, that I do not think the Postmaster General is treating the province of Ontario as fairly as he is treating other provinces. I am not going to say that he is doing that intentionally, but nevertheless, I think he is treating the province of Ontario unfairly, and I can prove, that from his own report. From 1895 to 1909, the number of post offices in the province of Ontario increased by some 17 per cent.
On what page?

I have only the report for 1909 where the number of post offices in each province is given. The report for 1895 shows that there were 3,138 post offices in Ontario while the report for 1909 shows that there were 3,694 post offices in Ontario. The number of post offices was increased in the different provinces from 1895 to 1909 as follows:

I can readily understand that in British Columbia and Manitoba there is a great need for an increase in the number of offices. The population has been increasing very rapidly, much more rapidly in those provinces than in any other, but I can understand also that apart from the consideration of the increase in population, there would be reasons why post offices v'ould have to be established in that country. The population is scattered. There are little sections here and there, and there is no doubt a necessity for even more post offices than you would naturally expect looking at the lump figures of population. But, there has not been such a great difference in the increase of population in the older provinces as would be indicated by the difference in the figures regarding the increase in the number of post offices. The figures of the census of 1901 do not show any such great difference in the increase of population in these provinces as would be indicated by the increase in the number of post offices. There is nothing to lead one to the supposition, for instance, that the population of Prince Edward. Island has increased to such an extent that the number of post offices had to be increased by 20 per cent while the population of Ontario increased to such an extent that the number of post offices only had to be increased by 17 per cent. The census of 1901 compared with the census of 1891 shoivs a decrease in the population of Prince Ed-w'ard Island. If the postmaster would consider the need for post offices as indicated from the amount of business done and from the standpoint of letters, post cards, registered letters, third and fourth class matter handled he would find no reason for any discrimination against Ontario; in fact, so far as third class matter is concerned Ontario furnishes 58 per cent of the total of the Dominion and of fourth class matter 61 per cent and compares favourably with the older provinces with regard to letters, post cards and other mail matter carried. I give these figures to the hon. gentleman because I want to show him that he would be justified in increasing the postal facilities of Ontario. Those figures show conclusively that in all fairness, if you consider population and business done, Ontario is entitled to a far greater number of post offices than it has at the present time, and I believe I have made good the point that Ontario is entitled to more post offices in order to put it on an equal basis with the other provinces. Then, I v'ant to impress upon the minister that there is a particular part of Ontario that is peculiarly entitled to his consideration and that part is the county of Frontenac. That has been the object of my argument here. I did not get up simply to find fault

for I am willing to say, as I believe, that a great deal has been done to improve the post office service of Canada. I am willing to give the Liberal party credit for the reduction of from 3 to 2 cents in the postal rate, but I do not believe the Postmaster General and his department are giving the rural part of the country the attention which it deserves. If the Postmaster General is depending solely upon the reports of inspectors of the various districts and if the inspector of the Kingston district has reported unfavourably on a daily service at Latimer post offices for instance, where they have a tri-weekly service, I think he has not given due' consideration to all circumstances. I am willing to depend upon the minister's judgment of'the matter and if he will consider it fairly and squarely I do not see how he can refuse to give these people a daily instead of a triweekly service. If the inspector of that district has reported to him against an increase in the service of that post office I say that he has proved thereby that he is not fit for the job he occupies. In the matter of carrying the mails I could give a great many instances from my own county where the people are performing a service for the public for practically nothing. For instance, take the Harrowsinith-Sydenham line. It is four miles there, four miles back, eight miles, six trips a week, forty-eight miles altogether and that service is performed for $48 a year. It is not costing you very much, Mr. Postmaster General. You are not going down in your pocket very deeply to pay for that service and I ask you to take that into consideration. But, I am pressing my claim on behalf of other parts of my county to have more frequent service than they are getting now. I could give many instances similar to that.
Let us take the Kingston-Sydenham line, 18 miles, 6 trips a week, 36 miles each day, making 216 miles. That man travels over
10,000	miles in a year, and he receives $257 for it. I think I am perfectly justified in asking that the cheapness of the service in the county of Frontenac should be considered in connection with my request for an extension of the service in the different parts of the county. I would also inform the minister that he can greatly improve the mail service in the county by increasing the number of accounting post offices and give them the right to issue and pay money orders. These accounting post offices are of very great convenience to the people of the country districts. I have collated the following statistics in reference to the accounting offices in Frontenac-the revenue received from them for the year 1905 was $5,900. salaries paid $3,904, postal notes and money orders paid $27,220, and postal notes and money orders issued $84,028. I give these figures to show that a considerable postal business is being done in the county, and I wish to tell the minister that if he increased the number of post offices in the county, it would correspondingly increase the amount of postal revenue. Many of these offices in Frontenac county are in centres where there are cheese factories and cheese business, and it would he a great convenience to the people if they were made accounting offices. I trust that the minister will give special attention to Latimer and Williamsville. I am satisfied that so far as the Latimer office is concerned, that a daily service will not add one cent of extra expenditure, because the increased revenue will pay the extra cost.

I agree with the hon. gentleman that Accounting offices are very convenient for the public, and where there is business enough to justify their establishment, the department as a rule does not object to them. I look upon the establishment of such post offices as a facility for the trade and industry of the country. As to the small amount paid to the mail-carrier, the hon. gentleman is aware, I suppose, that there are - many would-be mail-carriers who are dissatisfied because they did not secure the contract. As a rule we advertise these contracts, and we invariably accept the lowest tenderer, and I suppose the contractors know best what price they can do the work for. Now, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) should have confined his remarks to the county of Frontenac, and should not have alleged that preferential treatment was given by the Post Office Department as between different provinces. I can tell my hon. friend that I would be ashamed to preside over a department that would make any discrimination between one province and another. Every one knows that the banner province of the Dominion is Ontario.it is the richest, it is one of the oldest, it is the most populous, and it is entitled to all consideration from the Post Office Department, and from all other departments of the government. It has never entered into my mind that I should differentiate between one province and another. But we must admit one thing, the province of Ontario is an old and well settled province, offices have been in existence there for more than a century and there are fewer demands from that province for new offices than there are from the newer provinces. My hon. friend will be surprised to hear that in one constituency in Alberta, Medicine Hat represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Magrath) in the last year or two I have opened more than 80 post offices. Every one understands that, it is a new province, the distances are immense and there are groups of settlers established here and there and we must provide them with postal facilities, whereas Ontario is an old-established prov-

ince and therefore, fewer new offices are opened there. My hon. friend may say that fewer offices proportionately are opened in Ontario than in some of the newer provinces. True, I open fewer new offices in Ontario "because fewer are needed there as it has been so long settled, but when I am asked to increase the mail services in the rural sections of Ontario I always take into consideration in favour of that province its population, its wealth and its standing in the confederation. If my hon. friend will add together the various amounts represented by the mail contracts in Ontario he will see the difference there is between Ontario and Quebec for instance. At all events this question of differentiating between the several provinces does not enter my mind, and I should be ashamed as a public man to be guided Ly such considerations when the question of expenditure comes un. I take each case and judge it according to its own value, and to the best of my judgment in all conscience and honesty. My hon. friend mentioned a moment ago the Latimer post office. 1 rb.T''- Lie statements he made about thf jusj eetor are unwarranted.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: If the hon. member from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) thinks there can be absolutely no objection to allowing the Bill to go through, if every thing is killed that was objectionable, there ought to be no objection to our putting it through to-night.

There has been a great deal of discussion in connection with this Bill both in the Private Bills Committee and in the House. Having taken quite an active interest in opposing it in the Private Bills Committee, I was very anxious to have the objectionable features removed. The fact that the right hon. the Prime Minister has accepted the position taken by the hon. the leader of the opposition, removes, I think, the main objection-not that this Bill had anything to do with the damming of the St. Lawrence per se, but it added to the rights and privileges of the latter company, and consequently we decided on Monday last that, in according these additional rights and privileges, there should be some con-

cessions made by the company which was incorporated in 1901. There has been a good deal of play of words as to whether these two companies are identical. True each has a different corporate existence, but both are practically controlled by the same individuals. That was practically admitted by the hon. member for Lambtou (Mr. Pardee) when he introduced this Bill and agreed to amendments modifying the other. It was also admitted by the fact that the amendments proposed by the opposition were acceded to because they modified the Act of 1901. Unless the same promoters were behind both measures, the promoters of the present Bill would have no right to accept any amendments modifying the Act of 1901. There can be no doubt that the same individuals are behind both measures. The opposition was well timed and its efforts have been rewarded with a great deal of success. The integrity of_ the St. Lawrence river has been maintained by the opposition to this Bill. The hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) had made up his mind to accede to the demands of the St. Lawrence Power Company, and so had the International Waterways Commission.
Nothing of the kind.

There cannot be the slightest doubt that the three engineers of the Public Works Department condemned the scheme in 1908, in the strongest terms. If that was the case why did they modify their verdict in 1910, unless they were open to representations from the Minister of Public Works.
A very sad reflection upon the engineers.
Worse on the minister.
If he had made such representations, it would be worse.

These engineers have been often reflected upon. They were three engineers of the department who brought in a report on this Bill. One of them was Mr. Lafleur, chief engineer of the Public Works Department, on whom many reflections have been cast on account of dredging contacts which he justified as fair and reasonable, and which the Public Accounts Committee showed was clearly an imposition. Another is Mr. W. P. Anderson, engineer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Everybody knows that that department has not stood for efficiency in the past. Anything connected with it is rather suspiciously regarded by the public.
Not Mr. Anderson's branch.

There was Mr. Butler, a very eminent man, but when we consider that it was in his department the 212
Aylesworth canal was inaugurated, and put through, these men cannot be relied on as independent engineers.
Nonsense.
Mr. Butler was the head of the Department of Railways and Canals.
It was not Under him that canal wa3 started.

SHARPE It was under him it was perpetuated, and he still defends the whole enterprise. The whole discussion shows the necessity of an independent .board of engineers, occupying the same position as the Auditor General, so that they would not be subject to the suggestions or dictates of any minister, and could bring in an independent report the same as does the Auditor General.
. Mr. GRAHAM. You do not know the engineers.
The mere fact that the Minister of Public Works, when we had an all night session, said that he would see that tire public were protected, showed his inclination to support the enterprise.
I said in case there was any need for it.

It showed his leaning towards defending the whole proposition, and his anxiety to put it through. And I am inclined to think that, when the board of engineers brought in a modified report favouring the whole proposition- practically favouring it-that shows that there was some influence brought to bear upon them to amend their previous judgment. In 1908, they had condemned it in the strongest possible terms, but their second report reads as if they were trying to excuse and suggest a way around the difficulties presented in their previous report. However that may be, the acceptance of the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) removes the greatest objection to the Bill. It is true, there are still other objections. But I think the country will owe it to the opposition in this House that the integrity of the St. Lawrence river is maintained.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Will the hon. member (Mr. S. Sharpe) move his amendment?

In a moment. Last Monday, I suggested that, inasmuch as this same company was asking for privileges and powers from the government they should consent to a modification or revision of their rates by the Railway Board. I have given notice of an amendment that the rates of the St. Lawrence Power Company, incorporated in 1901, shall be subject to revision and supervision by the



Railway Board. I think that removes the other main objection. There is already a provision in this Bill giving the Board of Railway Commissioners control over the rates of this transmission company. But, if they had to pay high rates to the power company for their power, they could not give the public low rates. I understand that the promoters now are willing to accede to the request and make the rates of the power company subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. With these two amendments, I think the main features of the Bill are not so objectionable. I think the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) will agree with me that when the Bill was discussed in the Private Bills Committee it was agreed by Mr. McCarthy that they would buy their right of way and would not ask for easements from the farmers, as it vpas argued by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) that the farmers would be interfered with and their crops might be injured if only easements were secured. This point should be made clear in .the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is quite clear now.

In that case, there need be no objection to it. But some hon. members think it is not clear. There were two other amendments suggested. One was that the consent of the municipalities should be obtained before the company should have the right to construct their lines, and the other was that the assets of the province should not be expropriated without the consent of the province. I understand that the promoter of the Bill refuses to accede to these amendments. Of course, in that event, the government will have to assume the responsibility, so far as this House is concerned, of passing the Bill without these amendments.
If it passes.

Yes, if it passes. But, in m.v opinion, the main obieetionable features have been removed by acceding to the amendment of the leader of the opposition, and by the regulation of the rates of the power company. These two amendments, so far as I am personally concerned-and speaking for myself alone and no other hon. member-I have no objection to the Bill going through.

It has been suggested, as I understand, with references to this Bill, that the expectation of the company is to take power from the St. Lawrence Power Company which company it is claimed, has the right under the Act of 1901 to put dams in the St. Lawrence river at the head of the Long Sault rapids.
At the foot of the Long Sault?

Yes, at the foot of the Long Sault. I have thfe Act of 1901 incorporating the St. Lawrence Power Company. Now, I may read this statute quite wrongly, but as I read it, I cannot see that the St. Lawrence Power Company has any right whatever under the Act to construct any dams in the St. Lawrence river at the foot of the Long Sault rapids, or that it has any powers whatever, for it seems to me that the company is functus officio, not having carried out the provisions of its Act of incorporation. The Act provides:
The company may-	_
(a) manufacture, use, supply and dispose of electricity, water and gas, and water, hydraulic or other power by means of wires, cables, pipes, conduits, machinery or other appliances; and construct, maintain and operate works for the production, sale and distribution thereof, and for the purposes aforesaid may construct, acquire, use, maintain and operate canals, water-courses, raceways and water-powers in or adjacent to the St. Lawrence river on the north side thereof at any points eastward from Hoople's creek, in the county of Stormont, in the province of Ontario, to the eastern end of the Sonlanges canal.
That certainly does not give the company power to put dams in the St. Lawrence river at the foot of the Long Sault rapids.
Then these amendments will do no harm.

Certainly. not. Further, I cannot see-and I would like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) either now or at some other time, to explain the matter-how this St. Lawrence Power Company can construct dams at the point referred to. Section 13 of the Act provides:
The powers granted by this Act shall cease and he null and void unless works of the company capable of producing at least one thousand horse-power are completed within three years from the passing of this Act, and notwithstanding anything contained in any Act of parliament.
This company has not only not completed 'any works, but it has not begun any works. Surely, so far as the powers granted under this Act are concerned, this company is dead-it is finished. They would have to revive the Act, and for that purpose, to come to parliament.
Have they not constructed a portion of their works?

This company has constructed nothing. They did buy, I believe, some plant and property from Mr. M. P. Davis. But, surely, that is not a compliance with the provisions of this Act. The power plant which they bought from Mr Davis at the Long Sault rapids, and the power granted to this company is to con-

struct works at the Soulanges canal, which is a long way

Where is Hoople's creek?
Mr. GERMAN-I presume that it is somewhere near the Soulanges canal. But I do not know.
It is fifty miles away; it is west of the Long Sault rapids.
Above Dickinson's Landing.

So, this Act gives them power, so far as the parliament of Canada can give them power, to construct a dam at the Long Sault rapids, because the territory covered by their Act extends about 54 mi)es along the river.
Then, if they have complied with section 13, which I do not think they have done
They say they have.

I do not know what works they have completed for the development of 1,000 electrical horse-power. If they comply with that, then they are a live concern and can go on and develop power, a,nd _ if they can, my opinion is that this parliament should prevent them from putting dams in the St. Lawrence river, and tying up that river to this American corporation, allowing them to build their powerhouses on the American side of the river where this government cannot touch them. If any one suggests that this government can in any way control the output of power of that company, whose power-houses are on the United States side of the line, I fail myserf to see where any restriction can be imposed by this parliament. You can put any clause in the Act you like, they can violate that clause and use all the power on the United States side of the boundary line, and the only possible way of dealing with the situation would be for this government to blow up the dams with dynamite. I lor one am absolutely opposed to this company putting dams in the St. Lawrence river for that purpose, as long as we have ample powers in Canachk ;whieh are now being developed, and can be developed, to supply the necessities of this country.

I understood the hon. gentleman t-o say that in that Act they have not pow-er to construct any dam on the St. Lawrence. What construction does he put on clause 8, which reads as follows:
To construct, maintain and operate works for the production, sale and distribution (of electricity) .... and for purposes aforesaid may construct, acquire, use, maintain and operate canals, water-courses, raceways and water-power.
Now, how could they construct and make a water-power without a dam? If they have *212i
that right, surely it carries with it the right to dam the stream out of which the power is made.
All I can say is that if they have got that power, they should not have it, and that no plans submitted by them to the department should be approved of

'TAYLOR. I was not present to hear the Minister of Railways, but I read in the ' Hansard ' that he was strongly in favour of this Bill for the purpose of granting power that might be carried to the town of Brockville, where there is a large number of industries. I may say that I am largely interested in industries in the town of Brockville, employing some three or four hundred men the year round, and so far as our company is concerned, though we would be glad to get cheap power, we would be strongly opposed to getting it at the cost of great injury to the country and to other priavte interests. One of those interests is the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, a tremendous concern, having stock spread all over the country. If a dam was constructed that would injure the scenic beauty of the River St. Lawrence and the Long Sault, their stock would depreciate fully 50 per cent from the day the Bill was passed. The first report of the engineers said that it would damage the country away down to the city of Montreal. For this and other reasons, although I am largely interested in getting cheap power, I feel it my duty as a public man to oppose this Bill.
My hon. friend has perhaps not read all I said. This Bill has nothing to do directly or indirectly with damming the St. Lawrence.
As I read these Acts that are now in force, and this one in conjunction with them, it gives them that full power.
Not at all. My hon. friend is altogether mistaken.

I would like to know how this company is to get power to transmit electricity over its line unless they take it from the St. Lawrence Power Company? They have got no power plant in Canada excepting the power plant which they purchased from M. P. Davis, and which they would not assume to send, I apprehend, to Montreal. So what object can there be in giving this company the right to construct a transmission line when they have got tio power to send over the transmission line?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Did the hon. gentleman read the speech of the Minister of Railways?

I want to say that I am opposed in toto to the passage of this or any

similar Bill. One reason is because we have no right to lock up the water-powers of the country, and give them to any private individual or corporation. I think that is radically wrong and improper. Another reason is because the province of Ontario is developing this new policy with regard to water-powers, and if this or any other Bill passes, no matter with what restrictions, we give them corporate powers that will enable them to do something to hamper or interfere with that law against the interest of the province. Another reason is because it is an improper interference with provincial rights, and we have had too much of that lately. We have another Bill submitted to this House to-day for the incorporation of another power company between here and Montreal, and which I regard as equally objectionable with this one. We have had a great many of these Bills during the last two sessions, all aiming at getting control of the water-powers of this Dominion. And strange to say, all those men who are endeavouring to acquire that power or that control, when we analyse their companies, and get to the bottom of them, are Americans. If the information we have received be correct, they are part and parcel of a great combine that is trying to get control of every water-power in the United States and Canada, that they can lay their hands on. I think that is wrong. I never could understand why parliament should make or allow such a contact to be made as this government did with Mr. M. P. Davis, selling to him all the power of the Cornwall canal for a thousand dollars a year, a canal which is capable of generating several thousand horse-power, and then buying it back at $63 per horse-power, first binding this country for twenty-one years, and then extending that contract to eighty-four years. Consider how we are binding the interest of posterity. What right has parliament to tie up the property, the assets, of the province for that length of time, practically giving it in fee simply because there is a provision in that contract which enables them to renew it after that time has expired. After that contract was made, and extended in that way this Bill of 1901 was passed as a complement to it. The men who were interested in it control the two Bills to-day, and this Bill now before us is a complement of those two, and they desire to get it through for the purpose of using the same powers. If the information be correct that Mr. Davis has capitalized that contract, and sold it to Americans for a very large amount of money, according to reports all the way from $700,000 to $1,000,000, and they desire this Bill to help them to realize more out of it, and divide up what belongs to the country among Mr. SPROCLE.
themselves, then I say we are doing radically wrong when we give them the right to do that. Therefore, in my judgment, we ought to object in toto not only to this Bill but to any other Bill that has for its purpose to take over or control or utilize the water-powers of any province in the Dominion or to lease them for a great length of time. The province should do that, and should get whatever beneficial interest there is in these water-powers. These water-powers are the natural, inalienable assets of the provinces, and they should have the benefit of them. This federal parliament should not deprive them of this right, and we should not- give to any corporate body a right to interfere with or control them in any way, and for that reason, although in my judgment the amendments that are proposed would materially nullify some of the baneful features of this Bill, still I think we ought to allow no Bill of this character to pass, and I am just as much opposed to this as to any other Bill of a similar kind. I think we should oppose them all, and that we should not allow a single one to pass this House.

Before section 1 passes I want to say a word or two about this matter. The 'other night the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) replied very vigorously to some remarks that were made on this side of the House with reference to the position of the Hydro-Electric Commission. The First Minister seemed to think that it afforded a fruitful subject for vigorous retort because some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House thought well to point out that among other reasons why this Bill should not pass there was the fact that the province of Ontario has formed a scheme for supplying cheap power to the people, had worked upon that, had developed power to a very large extent in the west and that they were intending to develop it in the east as well. The Prime Minister argued very forcibly against creating such a monopoly as this would be. If a monopoly is advantageous to the people as this one is, it is not the kind of a monopoly that we should oppose. The Prime Miimter is quite right in saying that means should be afforded to the people to get power; if it does not interfere with navigation, at a cheap rate and if there is in any province no scheme inaugurated by the government to develop power it might be wise and right to allow a private company to develop that which manifestly would not otherwise be developed within a reasonable time. But in any province where they have inaugurated a scheme and actually put it in operation to supply power to the people every hon. gentleman in this House knows that no company can or will develop that power, and bring it to the people as cheaply as

will a properly conducted enterprise such as the Hydro-Electric Commission of the province of Ontario. It is the province of Ontario to-day, it will be the province of Quebec, or some other province to-morrow, or next year, and what I would urge upon the Prime Minister and the government is, that all things being equal, it is the duty of the federal power, instead oi opposing the provinces and setting themselves in opposition to them, as representing all the provinces, to afford every reasonable facility to them to develop power in the interest of the people. The province of Ontario has bona fide gone to work, and I think that, the other provinces will follow its example, to develop power and carry it to the people at cost price.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: They have not developed it in the east.

They are going to develop it in the east and I will guarantee they will develop it just as rapidly in the east as will this company' once they secure this monopoly. The St. Lawrence Power Company have had a good deal of time for developing but they have developed very little except schemes, one of which is the scheme that we now have before the House. Instead of coming to parliament under their own name openly and honestly and asking for an amendment to their Act they come under a subterfuge, under a disguised name and ask for powers which can be coalesced with the powers they got in 1901, and so, by the union of the two, get that which they otherwise could not get. The proposition we are up against now is this :	Shall we enact anything
that will enable these people more fully to accomplish a purpose which, if we had been alert in 1901, we would not have granted them the right to carry out. We never should have given them any powers, whatever and what I urge now is that we should not do anything that will entrench these people in a more formidable position than they occupy to-day. They dare not come to this House and ask for an amendment such as would represent, in effect, the Bill now before the House. They know perfectly well that if they came to this House and asked for any extension of their privileges, for the power of expropriation such as they intend to get under this Bill, the parliament of Canada dare not accede to their request. But they come under false pretenses, under an assumed name and they try by that means to deceive the public. I, for one. do not, any more than is unavoidable, intend to be a party to allowing these people to get by indirect and dishonest means that which they could not get and which we would not give them if they came honestly and openly and asked for it. If this coni pany came and asked us for such an extension of their rights as we will give them
by reason of this Bill, came and asked us for amendments which will give them in effect the rights that they will secure under this Bill, no gentleman, I venture to say, in this House, having regard for the interests of the people, would increase the evil that we created in 1901 by extending these additional privileges to this company. If we would not do that I-venture to say that it is not wise for us, it is not doing our duty, by these means to indirectly give this company rights which they could not get by way of an amendment if they came here asking for it. I was referring a moment ago to the question that even if the province" of Ontario were coming here we should not give them the right to dam the St. Lawrence river.
Even for the honest object of supplying the people with cheap power, we should not consent to the damming of the St. Lawrence. But when the province has entered on a scheme for supplying power to the people of Ontario at cost, and when we must recognize that the greater area and the greater the number of customers the cheaper can they supply that power, it is the duty of this parliament to see to it that we shall not set- up in competition a private company whose action in dividing the market must necessarily be to increase the cost to the people, by preventing the Hydro-Electric Commission from developing power as cheaply as they otherwise would. To test the honesty of this transaction, I say that if the promoter of this Bill will consent to put its expropriation provision on the same footing as in the former Act, we would then have an additional guarantee that this company would not by a side wind attempt to get an additional advantage. I tell the Prime Minister that the time will come and soon, when we will have to buy back from the company the rights which we injudiciously gave them in 1901. Just as wm will have to expropriate the Laurier hotel sooner or later, and pay an enormous price for our blunder in giving that park to a private company, so. sooner or later the people of Canada will demand that the company we authorized in 1901 to encroach upon the rights of the people, shall be expropriated and the people restored to their rights. If the government will persist in enforcing this Bill, and so entrench the St. Lawrence Power Company more firmly than they are entrenched under the Bill of 1901, then I shall have to demand the opinion of the House as to whether we shall have a provision controlling the rights of expropriation and the rights upon highways and the rights of entering upon private properties, which were limited in the Bill of 1901. That these two companies are identical there is no doubt; the argument has been' abandoned that they are not. They are the same people, but un-

fortunately they come to us under an assumed name. They have withheld as far as they could the knowledge of their identity, but step toy step, sometimes accidentally, we have developed our knowledge of them. Day after day and hour after hour as we have .been discussing it, more light has been shed upon this transaction, until we now know the _ fact, that these two companies are identical, and, worse still, that the backbone of the whole concern is an American institution which is exploiting this company, mainly in the interests of the United States. I can prophesy with almost certainty that in a year or two we will find we are making to-day a greater blunder than we made in 1901, and that these people will have a huge monopoly in the United States over the water-powers of the river St. Lawrence, interfering with our navigation and probably involving us in international disputes. And, Sir. we do not have to go far back to know how liable this government is, when it becomes an international issue, to bend the knee to the United States. It is only a month ago, since, figuratively speaking the Minister of Finance sat upon me because I tried to suggest that if the government went on with the French treaty they would likely be involved in complication with the United States. Our warning was set aside, and but a few Sundays ago we had these same gentlemen opposite, who so lately defied the United States, wending their way to Albany on that fateful Sunday morning.
Time.

And, forgetful of their duty to Canada they surrendering to the United States.
