I desire to call the attention of the minister to a petition which has recently been presented to him by, or on behalf of the outside .service of the City Post Offices. This petition is different from that discussed this afternoon, but It is quite as serious. I do not know how far the minister has yet been able to consider the matter, but I do hope that in justice to the large body of deserving civil servants who thus ask for justice, he will give favourable consideration to their petition. I am not in the habit of accepting petitions to present to this House without making some inquiry as to the merits of the cases involved, and with regard to the one Mr. LENNOX.
of which I am now speaking, I have taken some trouble to ascertain whether there was anything in reason in support of that petition in relation to the city, a portion of which I have the honour to represent. I do not for a moment say that because demands are made upon one of the departments, a member of this House should support those demands, but I really think there is a grievance here which is well deserving of the minister's favourable consideration. We have had in the past a great deal of discussion with reference to what has appeared to be a rather discriminating view taken of the rights of men of the inside service, as compared with those of men in the outside service. We know that in Ottawa, there may be a man in the inside service receiving for seven or eight hours' work a day a much larger salary than is received perhaps by his own brother in the outside serviec in this same city. It may even happen that the man in the outside service is the better man, but we constantly find that men in the inside service receive more for shorter hours than men in the outside service for longer hours. That has been demonstrated here over and over again. There may be reasons for this which the ordinary mind cannot grasp, but the fact exists. This discrimination exists in Ottawa, in Montreal, Hamilton, or any other city. That is at the bottom of the complaint that I wish to lay before the minister. I have looked into the cases of some 10 or 12 clerks in Hamilton, and I wish to present these to the consideration of the minister as an example of what is considered an injustice. If the minister can satisfy himself that there is no injustice, we must submit to that; I am simply laying these facts before him for his consideration, and I am sure that when he has considered them, he will endeavour to do justice. I have found that as regards certain employees, and I take long service men of good character in the post office at Hamilton-they are to-day in a class the maximum of which, under the statute, is $1,500 a year. I am prepared to admit that that may look a very nice salary to many people; thousands and hundreds of thousands in this Dominion would be glad to attain to that position. But I find that of all the men who have attained to two-thirds of that salary, $1,000, the majority have served in the Post Office Department for 30 years. After 30 years' service, they receive a salary of $1,000, and they are buoyed up by the wild hope that they may live long enough to get up to $1,500. That $1,500 is supposed to be a solace to these gentlemen, because there is a possibility of attaining it, there are great expectations before these valuable civil servants. I have here one man who for. three years has been receiving $1,000 a year. Before lie got to the $1,000 a year stage, he had served

*for 27 years. How would hon. gentlemen in this House, if they were starting life, care to look forward to 30 years of steady, good and faithful service with the hope that they might then get to $1,000 a year, and perhaps ultimately to $1,500 a year? I have here the names of men who have served for 28 years, 25 years, 30 years, 28 years, 28 years, 26 years, 25 years and 34 years. Of all these men, the highest stands to-day at $1,000. That man has served for that length of time after arriving at manhood. What expectation has he of ever reaching the maximum? 'Surely there must be something wrong in holding out an inducement to such a civil servant in the department that he may arrive at a salary of $1,500 a year. If, after 30 or 40 years, he receives only $1,000 a year, he must be a hopeful man if he thinks he will ever arrive at the maximum. These are the men of that class in the Hamilton post office, and I am taking the highest salaries in the class.
There are other men who have served 26 years, and have got to $900, others have served 24 years and 23 years and have reached $800; I just present these facts. I have no desire to take up the time of the House by commenting on them, but I ask the hon. minister to look at these men, not with bowels of compassion, because they are not beggars, they are just as good -men as those who sit in this House, just as honourable and well educated men, who have served their country faithfully, and who deserve better consideration-I ask the hon. minister to consider these men fairly as they would be considered by any wealthy employer, just as they would be considered by a big railway company, or any large institution of that kind. I think it might be well for the departments of this government to conduct their business as is conducted the business of our great corporations. The Postmaster General has on his staff a very good body of officers, the local inspectors, and I have no doubt that these do a great deal of work, and when men are to be promoted, their future, and the future of their families, so far as these depend on their salaries, is largely in the hands of these inspectors. I know that these inspectors are good respectable men, and capable officers, but there is precisely that same class in any large company. Every large company has that class of men who are the intermediaries between the employees, and the head of the department, just as those inspecting officers are the go-betweens between the staff and the minister, yet we all know that the president of a railway company, or the general manager systematically goes from year to year over the whole work from end to end, and gets in touch himself with the men who are reported upon by' these local inspectors.
I do not ask that the mighty minister of a
great Dominion should do this, but if it were possible for the minister, or his capable deputy, such as the Postmaster General has, to, season by season, go through the country, and get into touch with these people, see how they live, know what it costs them to live, that might do a great deal in harmonizing these differences and having justice done. I do not suppose that anybody understands better than the minister that since these scales of wages were arranged, there have been tremendous changes in the cost of living. Rent and food, and everything they have to pay for have gone up tremendously, far more 'than their wages, and I think that ought to be considered by the minister fairly and equitably. This country cannot stand extravagant salaries, but can stand justice to the men who serve it, and I hope that by some means it may be found possible for the deputy, or the minister himself, to get more in touch with the people who serve him, than has been the case in the past.

During'last session the hon. the Postmaster General brought down a Bill increasing the salaries of the letter-carriers, and the reason he gave was the increased cost of living. At that time I spoke in favour of increasing the pay of the railway mail clerks, and was assured by the hon. gentleman that during this session he would bring in a Bill regarding them. I have here a clipping from the Toronto ' Globe ' of February 10 last on that subject
Claims of Railway Mail Clerks.
The claims of the railway mail clerks is being pressed upon the government of Canada those claims are reasonable and urgent. For public service rendered in discomfort and danger the scale of remuneration is indefensibly low. The service is of such importance as to demand at all times physical vigour, intellectual alertness and training, moral integrity, and the strictest devotion to public duty.
The ceaseless strain of the work, due in part to the utterly improper type of mail cars in use on the railways, as the Civil Service Commission declared, ' tends to the shattering of the nerves and leads to other physical diseases, and to early disability.' Unless the remuneration is greatly increased it will be growingly impossible, under present conditions of service, to secure the type of intelligence and capacity made necessary by the examinations and required for the duties imposed. AVitk the cost of living steadily rising, the present low salaries will increase the temptation to dishonesty, a thing unjustified in any public service. Devotion to duty joined with capacity for service can find such abundant rewards in other positions that the mail service will be left for the culls and the derelicts unless reasonable increases are made.
Tiie f Globe ' does not hold to the view that civil service positions should in all things compete with the service of private corporations. But that does not mean that the salaries of those who carry on the public services should be held as near as possible to the star-

ration point. Those salaries should be reasonably adequate in all cases. In cases of special discomfort and of exceptional risk and danger, as with the railway mail clerks, the salaries should be even liberal. At the present time $400 as a minimum and $1,200 as a maximum is penurious for men doing responsible public service under conditions unattractive, uncertain, and full of peril. Substantial increases are due.
I think that when we expect to get any kind of good service from men in the position these occupy, a minimum salary of $400 is not in keeping with their work. A man commencing in the position of letter carrier to-day would earn in the neighbourhood of $600 per year, and I think that an increase to them, of say, $200 a year all thrpugh, and raising their pay from_year to year, so as to allow them to go to the same limit as first-class clerks in the Post Office Department, namely $1,500, would be only a fair thing to do. Would the Postmaster General be good enough to let us know whether he can take that up this session or not.	_

Let me outline briefly what has been the policy of the department with regard to the proposed increase. First. I must say to my hon friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that he does not appeal in vain when he prefers a request in favour of that class of the post office employees to which he has referred. I have already stated in this House that I am mvself the son of an old civil servant, who has been in the active service for now over forty-seven years and who has raised a family of ten children. I happen to know something about the increased cost of living during the last 25 years and what changes have taken place in every-day life. I may say that, since I took office in 1906, I have done my little share toward improving the condition of the employee. The House will remember that when I was made Postmaster General, the minimum salary of our postmasters was only $25 I made an increase and brought the minimum up to $35. Last year, at the request of several hon. members, and of the civil servants themselves, I went very carefully into the condition of the humbler class of post office employees, the sorters, stampers and labourers employed in the city post offices. pressed publicly on several occasions their deep sense of gratitude to the government and to the department in particular to the very substantial increase which this parliament voted last year in their favour. But now I am confronted with another request, from the hon. member for East, Hamilton (Mr. Barker), my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Russell), and, I may say, from nearly all the members-who represent the larger postal districts in Canada. Petitions have poured in upon the department, during the _ last two months, asking that the railway mail clerks should receive a substantial increase. Since these petitions began to come into the department, an agitation has gone on amongst another class of employees, the clerks in the city post' offices. I have stated, and I repeat, that, in my judgement the members of the outside service in the larger post offices, such as those of Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Quebec, Vancouver and Victoria, should be placed on the same basis as tire members of the inside service at Ottawa. That is my personal view, and I know that it is shared by a large number of members of this House. But; for the present, all I can say is, that, in my opinion, the day

is not far distant when all those who serve in the outside service in these large city post offices will have to come under the Civil Service Act as introduced in this House two years ago and is now wTorking so well for the Civil Service at Ottawa. I intend, during the recess, with my deputy and my officials, to prepare a classification in order to bring in the members of the outside service in these large offices. province leaving a surplus from that province alone of $3,273,000. I would like the minister to tell the committee why it is that the total expenditure in 1902 only amounted to $3,888,000 while in 1909 it was increased to $7,401,000, or an increase of nearly half within the past seven years. He does not need to tell us that these 650 post offices that he has established cost anything like the amount of money that the total incre.ase in the expenditure represents. Let him give us some good reason why the post office expenditure has increased until to-day it is $3,523,417 more than it was seven years ago. There are some suggestions that I wish to make to the Post Office Department, and which 1 feel justified in making because they are in the public interest. There should be a system of rating post office employees as to efficiency and faithfulness.
Then the salaries should be rated on the basis of the quantity of the work the employees perform, their accuracy in doing it, and their compliance with the postal regulations. office rules, and conduct, their punctuality and regularity in attendance, and their familiarity with the regulations, and instructions regarding their duties. How important it is that in our towns and smaller cities these officials should be put under some form of discipline. Then, it has been brought to the attention of par' liament that post offices are built in this countrv without the knowledge of the Postmaster General, and without consideration of the postal needs of the district. The svstem now is that the Minister of Public Works receives petitions from his followers. and if he deems it wise in the interest of the Liberal party in the district, he erects a post office without any regard to the proportion between the income received from the place and the cost of the building. I believe that in the erection of post office buildings, the Post Office Department should have a voice. The Post Office Department has trained agents who should be familiar bv experience and observation with the requirements of the postal service in all directions, and it is the post office officials who should select the site and arrange for the interior equipment of the building. Sites for public buildings to be
used exclusively for the Post Office should be selected by the Postmaster General, and in case a building is erected for the joint use of the Post Office and other departments, the approval of the plans and the specifications and estimates as to space, interior arrangement and equipment should be furnished by the Postmaster General. That is the common sense business way of looking at the question, but instead of that the Minister of Public Works, who knows little or nothing about the needs of the postal service, proceeds to erect post office buildings which are beyond the require-ents of the post office district, and the Postmaster General knows nothing about it. A further suggestion which I have to make is that the mails should not be delivered by city carriers except at residences and city-offices where approved mail receptacles are provided at the door or entrance. This would effect a. great saving, because the delay in city delivery is one of the obstacles which the Post Office has had to contend with. It has been estimated that there is a loss of 15 seconds at each place of delivery, and if there are 336 stops, which is the average number, there is a loss of one and a half hours a day for each carrier. Hence a quicker delivery by the means suggested would save to the country many thousands of dollars. Then, another suggestion is that when the writer of a letter on which the postage is prepaid shall endorse on the outside his name and address, such letter shall not be advertised but shall remain uncalled for at the office to which it is directed the time the writer may request or the Postmaster General would prescribe, and it shall be returned to the writer without additional postage, and if not delivered treated as a dead letter. Then, another important suggestion is that no employees of the Post Office shall canvass or solicit votes, accept the position of poll clerk or scrutineer, and that they shall not in any way encourage or take part in a political campaign under the penalty of losing their business. I have a letter here from an eastern town in which the postmaster appears to have been dismissed because he did not solicit votes for the Liberal candidate. The Postmaster General knows that year after year we have called his attention to the fact that the weekly press throughout [DOT] this country had been most unfairly dealt with, and while he may say he has stopped to a certain extent some of the papers coming in from the other side, at the same time lie has let down the bars and allowed in some of the most corrupt literature from the old land, and cheap publications of different kinds. At the same time he has shut out valuable magazines and periodicals of an educative character that would be of great help to our people. The Postmaster General has absolutely forgotten the use of the mails. The franking privilege, as used by the departments, is open to serious criticism. The Postmaster General remembers that the franking system in force under this government has received very serious criticism from members on this side. Tons of political mail matter leave the departments to assist and promote one interest, the continuance of this government in office. The Post Office Department should make every other department give a definite statement of the amount of mail matter sent -out by it. I might go on making suggestions, but I merely wish to devote the rest of my time to a matter which I believe is of greater interest to the people, especially those living in the rural districts. In the Saturday Evening Post, of February 19. 1910, that paper said:
Rural free mail delivery lias proved to be the most popular and beneficent branch of the whole postal service.
I know that if the Postmaster General had investigated the benefits derived from rural free mail delivery in the United States, Germany, France and England, he cannot come to any other conclusion than that the day is not fat distant when he will be compelled to take a different position on this question. Instead of saying we will have to wait until we have a population of 20,000,000, he will find that in a very few years demands will come from the people in the thickly settled portions of the different provinces for this great convenience. To-day the minister cannot fail to see that the people are anxious that this service should be granted them. I know that all kinds of letters are pouring into his department and all kinds of criticisms are showered on him because of the paltry system he has now under way. That system simply means that the mails will only be delivered on existing mail or stage routes, and then only to certain portions of the country. But have not the people on the other concessions just as good a right to the advantages of rural free maii delivery as those who reside on existing mail or stage routes? Whv should the men on these routes have their farms increased in value, as they undoubtedly are, by their
enjoyment of the advantages that come from the delivery of the mails at their very door, and the people who live a mile or so away, perhaps in a more thickly settled portion of the country be deprived of these advantages? Let us look at what is being done in this regard. The Minister, on November 30, stated that he had 302 routes in operation, as I understand from the return on page 5883 of ' Hansard.' Last year I received a return on J anuary 27, in which the minister distinctly stated that the 44 rural mail routes then in operation only cost this government $663.50, or -an average of about $15 per route. Multiply the 302 routes not existing by 15 and you have an expenditure of only $4,530. Let us see where these 302 routes are located. In little Prince Edward Island there are 33; in New Brunswick, 15; in Kingston district, 23; in Toronto district, 38; in London district, 104; in Winnipeg district, 28; and I find away up in Edmonton, 13. How then can the minister hope to make the people believe that the system he has inaugurated has taken out of the Post Office Department any large amount of money-$4,530 according to that estimate. He does give an estimate here showing that the total increase in the cost of the mail service, including the service of rural delivery boxes for four years-I cannot understand why he puts in the four years-amounts to $55,000, when, according to his estimate of last year, the cost was only $4,500. I am well aware that if he will give rural free mail delivery as it ought to be given to the thickly settled portions in the older districts of Ontario and the other provinces, he will find that the expense will increase. But he will also find that in these provinces there is no great extent of territory that can be possibly covered by it. In the United States .this system is governed strictly by regulation. It is impossibly to have a route established there unless there are 100 families in the 24 miles, which is the standard route, and the shorter routes are compelled to have a proportionate number of families. 85 out of that 100 are compelled to distinctly contract to take the mail delivery at their do-ors and erect the boxes there. But I need not go further in the discussion of this subject as that has been gone over so many times before, but I want to call the attention to the fact that the time has come in some of the older provinces when the population is decreasing yearly instead of increasing in the rural districts. Take the province of Ontario, the deputy minister of that province made the statement that while in 1889 the population w'as 1,108,874 in 1899 it was only 1,047,016, showing a reduction of 61,858. The cities have increased in numbers but not the rural districts, and many people from the rural districts have gone to the Northwest where they can get the advantages which they do

not enjoy in the older provinces, and which advantages are a great inducement to people to remain on their farms. I appeal to the right hon. the Prime Minister to investigate this subject in so far as the thickly settled districts are concerned. We are not asking for rural free mail delivery in the partially settled districts nor are they asking for it in those districts in the United States, but the day is at hand when we must give to the people in the rural districts every advantage to induce them to remain on the land-not only telephones and electric cars, but free mail delivery at their doors. The expense of running a farm is far in excess of what it was years ago, and takes a lot of money to get the mails, especially when wages are so high as they are at present. Rural free mail delivery will bring the farms and rural communities in closer connection with commercial centres. It encourages the improvement of country roads, and by making rural life more attractive it stimulates agriculture. It has been the means of increasing the value of farm lands and has materially reduced the number of postoffices throughout the United States. While in the United States the number of post offices in the year 1900 was 76,688, this number has graduallv been reduced, until in 1909 the United States has only 60,155 post offices. Therefore when the hon. gentleman talks of the deficit in the United States postal revenue and says that is due to rural free mail delivery, lie should also take into consideration the great reduction in the number of post offices. While in the Dominion the number of post offices has increased, we find that in the United States, with its increasing population, the number has been cut down this last year by some 1,100 post offices. They saved, thereby, as distinctly stated in their report, $92,000. But the minister, with his present system of rural mail delivery cannot cut off any post offices, apparently. Taking the average increase in post offiees previous to the establishment of rural free delivery there would be at present upwards of 100,000 post offices in the United States. The annual saving made through the reduction in cost of buildings, maintaining the 40,000 post offices with postmasters would still further reduce the deficit attributed to rural free delivery to something like $5,000,000. The installation of rural free delivery is followed by an increase in the amount of mail delivered, and collections. Such increase is not credited to rural free delivery. Additional evidence of the increase of the amount of mail passing through rural delivery is furnished in the fact that only 992 routes handled 25,000 or more pieces of mail during the three months ended June 80. 1907, and 3,232 routes
25,000	or more during the three months emjed May 31, 1909. In 1907, 27 routes Mr. ARMSTRONG
handled more than 50,000 pieces of mail, during the quarter ending June 30. In 1909, 95 routes more than 50,000 during the quarter ending May 31. On 35 of these routes the value of the stamps on mail collected for the period indicated exceeded	$200. On 24 routes this
item exceeded the carriers' salary. Page 4 of the fourth assistant Postmaster General's report gives a list of these routes showing the number of pieces handled, and the value of postage on mail matter collected during the three months ended May 31, 1909. On June 30, 1909, the service was in operation on 40,628 routes, and 40,499 carriers were employed. During the year 4,115 new routes were established. In 840 counties in the United States the service had been adjusted on June 30, 1909, so as to furnish rural delivery to the greater portion of the rural population. During the year 1909, 1,149 post offices were discontinued, the patrons of which are now served by rural free delivery, thereby effecting a reduction in the expenditure on the postal service of $92,000. There has been unprecedented improvement in the condition of roads traversed by rural carriers due to the intelligent and well directed interest of postmasters and carriers. The average increase of mail handled on rural mail routes of the United States in the last four years was 55 per cent in the average number of pieces of mail handled by a" carrier. It is estimated that the daily travel of the carriers on routes now in operation aggregates
980,000	miles. Rural free delivery serves 20,000,000 people. The annual expenditure in 1905 for services in the post offices, salaries of postmasters, salaries of clerks, &c., city delivery not including railway mail service, or rural delivery service, or transportation, amounted, in 1906, to $51,000,000, while in 1909 it was over $102,000,000, an increase of $51,000,000-just double. The rural free delivery was not responsible for the increases in any of the branches I have suggested.
Last year, the minister said that 44 routes had been established in Canada, and the cost to the department had been only $663 per annum. The minister must remember that our largest immigration is coming from the United States, a country almost completely covered with rural free delivery routes. And if he will not undertake this work of free rural delivery these people will naturally hesitate before leaving the many advantages they now enjoy to be compelled to live in a country where such advantages are not even recognized. Let the minister appreciate this fact, that the United States has 40,000 rural free delivery routes in operation serving 20,000,000 of people. The system covers one million miles of road; the carriers cover 200,000,000 miles of road

each year, and handle over 200,000,000,000 pieces of mail.
I do not wish to take up further time, though the subject is such an important one. The present system of rural free delivery established by the Postmaster General merely leads to the creation of contention and strife in the rural districts. If he will go into the rural districts where these routes are in operation to-day, he will find that the people using them would not think of parting with the service, on the contrary he would find dissatisfaction and discontent in the districts that are not receiving these valuable services.
I trust the Postmaster General will take into serious consideration tlie suggestions I have made, and also that he will go throughout our land and investigate this question-not only the complaints he has heard here to-day, but will go into the rural districts and learn, as he surely will learn there, that the thickly-settled portions of the older provinces are most emphatically and earnestly ready to receive rural free delivery.

I desire to say a word on behalf of the clerks employed in the city post offices, whose case has been already referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Russell), and others. I think there are no clerks in the Civil Service so poorly paid as the clerks I have referred to. I agree with the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) that the Bill brought down last year dealt pretty fairly with the letter-carriers. But when the Postmaster General passes over the clerks employed in the city post offices and gives increases to the inspectors, assistant inspectors and men of that class-I am not finding fault with these increases; I am glad these gentlemen have got them-but when the hon. gentleman failed to remodel the salaries of these clerks he passed over a class of civil servants who much more needed an increase. I was much pleased to hear the Postmaster General himself admit that these clerks were not sufficiently paid, and state also that he intended at some future time to consider an increase for them. But they are not a very numerous class, and I do not think it would mean a very big task for his department to take into consideration the increase of salaries for that class of clerks. Some of these men have been in the service for from 25 to 35 years and are receiving now only $1,000. In the Hamilton post office there are among the clerks there men qualified to hold any position which might come their way, some of as clever clerks, I think, as can be found anywhere, and yet kept at a salary of $1,000. after, perhaps, 35 years work. The railway mail clerks are asking
for an increase, and I should be glad to see them receive it. But I think that the clerks to whom I have referred are entitled to as high a salary as the railway mail / clerks, who are off for one, two or three days in the week. I think that if the Postmaster General would take into his serious consideration the advisability of giving an increase to this class of civil servants he would be easily able to see his way to doing it at this time. I hope the minister will consider it and not put off the granting of this increase to another session.

Some time ago I wrote to the Postmaster General, inclosing copies of the 'Air Brake' magazine, a publication purely educational in the interests of railway men. The air brake, as the minister knows, is The apparatus which controls the speed of trains. Those in charge of this magazine believe that every railway man should have all possible information and instruction concerning this device. If these magazines' were admitted free of postage into Canada, or under reduced postage rates, they would reach a large number of railway men who would be in a position to take advantage of the instruction the magazine contains. Has the minister finally decided what he will do in the premises?

If this publication, the ' Air Brake Magazine,' which I am sure is very useful to railway men, comes under the ordinary regulations, it should be admitted at one cent a pound. I am glad my hon. friend has brought this1 matter to my notice. I take a great deal of interest in these technical magazines, because of their educational character, and I desire to encourage their reading. I will have further inquiry made into the matter, and give my hon. friend an answer on Monday. I see nothing in the character of the paper which would prevent it from Cuming under our classification, which would admit it at the special rate existing between the two countries. Now I will say to my hon. friend the junior member for Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) that the question of raising the salaries of post office employees has been occupying the attention of the department for several weeks. We have dealt this session with the class of employees I referred to last night. The resolution giving another scale of salaries to superintendents, railway mail clerks, post office inspectors, assistant inspectors, and assistant postmasters has been accepted by the House. This is as much as we can do this sftsion. But I have pledged myself that between now, and the next session of parliament I will see that a proper classification is made of the outside service in the larger cities, and will try to bring them' under the very efficient legislation known as the Civil Service

Act which was introduced two years ago by the Minister of Agriculture.
Now, Sir, I will not attempt to answer all the questions raised by the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) this evening, because he has evidently prepared a very able brief on the' whole range of postal questions. I must congratulate him on his address, and on his industry. Evidently he has found inspiration in the literature published in the United States. It is part of my duty to read that literature carefully. My hon. friend makes a mistake in comparing the two countries, especially on that vexed question of second class matter. I know as a matter of fact that a long investigation has taken place in the United States as regards the transportation of certain second-class matter by railway companies. My hon. friend asked whether I knew that in the United States something like $69,000,000 have been charged to the United States exchequer, to the dismay and surprise of the Washington authorities, because it had been practically a robbery from the people. Well, my hon. friend has unwittingly made a mistake in comparing Canada with the United States as regards second class matter. The system we have in this country is entirely different from that in the United States as regards the transportation of second-class matter by railway companies. That matter in the United States is transported according to weight, at one cent a pound, whilst in this country we have a mileage basis. For instance, a baggage car service costs the country four cents a mile, a postal car service costs eight cents a mile. That is the basis of the expenditure for the transportation of second-class matter from one end of the country to the other. Is our system much better than the United States system? Certainly it is, from a post office point of view. I have here an extract from the evening 'Journal,' of New York, of February 5, 1910, in regard to the investigation which was recently held in that country. The title reads, ' Another polite question to Mr. Taft.' .
Mr. Taft, our president, said that the people were subsidizing magazines because the mail carried magazines for a cent a pound, and he said they actually cost the government nine cents a pound to carry the magazines.
That is where the robbery takes place, it is done by weight, whilst in this country we have a uniform basis of a mileage system with the railway companies.
We would like to ask Mr. Taft one question. You say that the United States government loses $64,000,000 a year because it carries second-class mail matter, magazines, and so on, for one cent a pound. Do you know that in Canada the post offices carry second-class mail matter for a quarter cent a pound and makes a profit of a million dollars a vearr Mr. LEM1EUX.
That is the opinion of an American newspaper on the two systems.
Is it true?

It is perfectly true, so much so that at present the railway companies of Canada, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Grand Trunk railway are knocking at the door of the Post Office Department in order to obtain a new basis of mileage. They say they are losing money, that to-day their mail cars are filled with such matter, and that they receive only the same amount of money as if they were empty.
Are those roads running to the west on long hauls through the western districts, filled with second-class matter?

If my hon. friend could see them at this season of the year, when immigrants are coming into the country, or during the Christmas season, and the Easter season, if he could see the mail cars of the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Canadian Northern he would be surprised. The system is completely different in the United States, and the tendency in that country to-day is to adopt the Canadian system. Once more they have to come to Ottawa to learn something in business management.
How are the railway companies paid for carrying mail matter- by the car or by the pound?
They are paid on a mileage basis.
You pay no more for a full car than for one half full?
No.
You have the use of the whole car if you want it?
W'e have the use of the whole car.
And you pay so much per mile whether the car is empty or full?

I said a moment ago that we paid four cents a mile for a baggage car and eight cents a mile for a postal car. Some of the companies carry mail at the rate of two or three cents a mile. This rate is given under old contracts which were made before confederation and which have been continued since, but the regulation to-day is four cents a mile for a baggage car and eight cents for a postal car.

I wish to ask the minister a question with reference to mail-cars. He says that we are charged eight cents a mile for a postal car. It should be a postal car, in my judgment, up to a certain standard where the occupants would be comfort-

able and would have suitable conveniences to enable them to do their work. How many new mail cars have been built and placed on railway postal routes in Canada during the past five years? Where are they in use? What reports or complaints have been made to the department or superintendent of the railway mail service by railway mail clerks in regard to the unfitness of the mail cars during the last year, or the last six months? Have there been any, and, if so, how many complaints that the health of the railway mail clerk suffers from the unsuitableness of the cars they occupy while discharging their duties? Have complaints been macjg as to the imperfect. heating of these cars, and are the railway companies building, with any degree of rapidity, new and suitable cars for the mail routes that are used to-day?
A similar question, perhaps not so complete, was asked the other day, and I gave the answers. It is on ' Hansard.'
I put that question, but it was very much narrower.	,

If the hoi), gentleman will put his question on the order paper, I will be very pleased to give a proper answer. I know that the railway companies ha,ve improved the standard of the mail car. We have made representations to them during the last three or four years. When I was Minister of Labour I did remonstrate with some of the companies which really were not giving our railway ftiail clerks the accommodations that they were entitled to as human beings. There are a number of difficulties which cannot be easily overcome. For instance, the railway mail clerks were asking that the mail car should be placed at the end or the centre of the train instead of next to the locomotive. Well, that is a difficult question. The mails have to be delivered at a certain point on the platform, and it would create delay and cause trouble in the service. But, as regards the hygienic conditions, the railways have manifested a very sincere desire to improve the condition of the cars. I cannot state the number of cars built on the new system within a year or two, but I will get the statistics at a later stage.
I merely read these questions so that they will be on ' Hansard,' and so the minister will be enabled to answer them later.

The hon. member for Lambton opened his remarks by stating that advertisements were appearing in a paper called the ' The Canadian Farm.'1 I am glad that my hon. friend brought that paper to the notice of the House. The ' Canadian Farm ' is owned by a well known Conservative in Toronto, and it has 213
a large circulation amongst the farmers of Ontario. It is a proper medium in which to insert advertisements of the post office for rural services in the districts adjoining Toronto. I do not think that fault should be found with our department for choosing that medium for advertising purposes. The hon. gentleman says : You have a surplus; cannot you give some increase to your railway mail clerks? I think I have answered that question to the satisfaction of the hon. gentleman. My hon. friend spoke of the expenditure in the Yukon district, and compared it with the expenditure of other sections.
In Dawson city.

In Dawson city. Well, we must take a broad view of this subject. It is all very well to say that we draw hardly any revenue as compared with the expenditure in the Yukon territory, but
1	claim it as a matter of pride for Canada that one can send a letter from Halifax to Dawson at two cents whilst a letter sent from Dover in England across the channel to Calais would cost five cents. It is true that we do not derive a large revenue from the Yukon district, but the Canadian mails are just as safe in that district today as they are in the city of Toronto or the city of Ottawa. In the Yukon district we have a large settlement composed of miners. We have a service equal to that in any other section of the country. With the fair surplus we have I think it is only right that we should give our hardy Canadians who have been settling and opening that district to civilization a proper mail service. It costs some money-$140,000 a year. For the railway mail service alone across the White Pass we have to pay something like $60,000 a year. That is the only accessible route through which our mails can pass, and I must say to my hon. friend that not only is the Yukon service a service for Canada but partly for the United States. We are spending some money in Dawson. We pay the postmaster $5,000 a year but Mr. Hartman, the postmaster, with $5,000 receives less than some postmasters who are paid $2,000 or $1,500 in this section of the country. My hon. friend knows that rental, provisions and clothing in the Yukon cost twice and thrice as much as in other sections of this country. My hon. friend says that there has been an increase in the expenditure. That I do not deny. It must be remembered that the inland letter rate has been reduced from 3 cents to 2 cents; the letter rate from Canada to the United States reduced from 3 cents to
2	cents; the letter rate from Canada to Great Britain and all other portions of the British empire reduced from 5 cents to 2 cents, and the rate on drop



letters for city delivery reduced from 2 cents to 1 cent, which is the lowest rate for this service in any country in Europe or America. Then again, the rate on Canadian newspapers and periodicals sent from publishers in Canada to subscribers in Great Britain and every part of the British empire has been reduced from 3 cents per pound to \ cent per pound, and the rate on Canadian newspapers and periodicals sent from publishers in Canada to subscribers in Great Britain and every part of the British empire, has been reduced from 2 cents per pound to I cent per pound, and the rate on Canadian newspapers and periodicals sent by the general public in Canada to correspondents in Great Britain and all parts of the British empire has been reduced from 8 cents a pound to 4 cents.	The reduction in the rates on
newspapers sent by publishers in Canada to subscribers in Great Britain tends to a wider dissemination of Canadian newspapers and other publications and has made better known to the world the wealth and industries of Canada. Then, the parcel post rate between Canada and Great Britain formerly provided that a parcel not exceeding 3 pounds in weight would cost 1 shilling and the scale ran up to XI pounds for 3 shillings. Now, on Canadian parcels to the United Kingdom the rate is brought down to 12 cents a pound. The Canadian 'Gazette' commenting on these reduced rates says:
Those reductions are a welcome sequel to the penny post, and must^ cut yet deeper the channels of closer connection.
My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) spoke about the rating of our post office employees and I may tell the hon. gentleman that every man is traced in the Post Office Department from the day he enters it to the day he leaves. As to the city post offices we have monthly reports from our inspectors and I think it may be said that we follow very closely our employee. I may also tell my hon. friend that I have given notice as publicly as possible that the employees must not take part in politics; that they must do their duty towards the country that pays them and that they jeopardize their positions if they take an active part in politics. My hon. friend knows, my views on rural mail delivery, and I think it may be said that our system has made fair progress since its establishment. We have made a modest beginning and we are proud of it because it is working smoothly and well. We have quite a large number of routes in the province of Ontario. I do not believe that we should have supplied the farmers with free boxes because I think it would be imprudent on our part and it would be beneath the dignity of the farmers to accept Mr. LEMIEUX.
them on such conditions. Under the present condition the farmer pays the cost price of the box and he gets a good service. Let me point out to the hon. gentleman that in the United States last year the postal receipts amounted to $203,000,000 and the expenditure to $221,000,000. My hon. friend says that the rural mail delivery has done away with many post offices in the United States, and while that may be true the fact remains that in the United States, with their very extensive system of rural mail delivery, they rolled up last year the handsome deficit of $17,441,000. I do not think we can afford to follow the example of the United States in maintaining such an expensive luxury. We are going on quietly and gradually in Canada and I think we are on the safe side. . The time will come when we will have a large population in this country, and if the Post Office Department is administered as well then as it is now it may be taken for granted that we will have King Edward boxes at the door of every farmer in Ontario and the western provinces. Our post office revenue last year was $7,401,000 and our expenditure $6,592,000. For my part I would rather keep within these conservative lines than go the pace they have gone in the United States which would no doubt result in a comparatively equally large deficit.
Does the minister seriously think that with our population of 7,000,000 and their population of 90,000,000 Ve would lose in proportion the same amount of money as they did?

We have a small population and a small revenue compared with the United States but we have at the same time a larger territory than they have. The expense is not in the box itself, that is a very small matter, but it is in the laying of the route, in getting new routes and new couriers, and giving out new contracts to cover that immense territory. That is where the cost comes in. From the figures I gave the House the other day, my hon. friend will find that the increase in the expenditure under the head of rural mail delivery in my department comes from the fact that we have been obliged to do away with the existing mail service as between one office and another office and replace it by another service to cover each box on the route. That costs three times as much. As our territory is as large as or larger than the United States, if we were to go on with the system as lavishly as the United States has gone it would cost the country too much money and I wish to remain on safe lines.
In conclusion I wish, to say that this department has been well administered by my predecessor, Sir William Muiock,

and it shall be my ambition in the future to administer it as well as he did; my only ambition is to follow in his footsteps.

The method of rural delivery is not applicable to all parts of the country. I have in mind routes in my constituency where the route is from 40 to 50 miles in length, and a good deal of the travelling by the courier is done at night. It would be impossible for him to open the boxes along his scattered route and deliver the mail to the people and reach the end of his route in any reasonable time. Where the country is laid off like a checkerboard and thickly settled and the routes short the system may be applicable, but I do not think it can apply to certain districts I have in mind. Of course this is our misfortune, but I think some consideration should be given to the distances between post offices. I have been told by officers of the department that the rule is to place post offices not closer together than four miles. Two miles is a long distance for a farmer to travel every day for his mail. If it is impassably, to accommodate these people by rural mail delivery, I would suggest that the minister should increase in those places the number of post offices. It does not cost much to furnish a post office and it is a great accommodation to the people, because it lessens the distance to be travelled. I find that it is difficult to obtain the rural mail delivery because one applicant does not count, you must secure a large number. I believe a majority along the route, to apply for the accommodation . before you can get it. Take for example a route 50 miles long with 100 or 200 families living along it. Who is to organize the application, who is to find out h'ow manv people will take the boxes and join in the system? It is an impossible task for the individual farmer or resident who desires to secure the accommodation. I have had applications of that kind and have had to tell the people that they must get a majority along the route to join before they could get the accommodation of rural delivery boxes. It would take weeks and months to canvass and ascertain if it would be possible to secure that number. I trust the minister will take into consideration the necessity of revising his rules with regard to the distance between post offices. So as to give the people in the country districts more accommodation.

What is the department doing in the matter of a largely signed petition from Central Park asking for an inquiry into the circumstances connected with the closing of that post office? This petition was addressed to the department in February last, and bore 175 signatures of persons who had been deprived of 213*
their mail facilities by the action of the department.
The facts are not fresh in my mind.

I think this matter should receive the minister's personal attention. Last summer I wrote a personal letter to the minister and Mr. Cowan also wrote. To these letters we received no reply, except an acknowledgment from an official of the department, saying that the letters would be submitted to the minister on his return. That post office had been established for 14 years, but now it has been closed, depriving about 300 families of their postal facilities. I know that the-facts have been misrepresented to the department, and it was because of that knowledge that I addressed a personal letter to-the minister. I regret to find from the minister's lack of knowledge to-night that the matter has never come to his attention at all ynd that he knows nothing about the subject. The matter originated through a comniaint from residents of Central Park against the management of the post office there. For several years the inspector has been reporting to the department that the post office was mismanaged. For at least four years these complaints went on without action, the then postmaster was allowed to continue in office and the dissatisfaction continued; but finally last summer the matter seems to have been brought to a crisis by the receipt of a largely signed petition asking the Postmaster General to investigate the matter. Then the Postmaster General wrote, not to the inspector or to any person in authority there, not to the member for New Westminster or the member for Vancouver, whose districts this post office serves, hut to a gentleman whose existence I heard denied in this House this afternoon. This letter was addressed by the deputy minister to this gentleman, who, we were assured this afternoon, had ceased to exist-the administrator of the patronage of the department for the district of New Westminster.
Post Office Department. Ottawa,
June 28, 1909.
Robert Jardine, Esq., .
New Westminster.
Who was he?

He is the gentleman who aspired to the position I occupy just now, hut whose aspirations were disappointed :
Dear Sir,-I beg to draw your attention to the communication addressed to you on the 25th ult., on the subiect of the postmastership of Central Park, and asking you to nominate some suitable person who could be appointed to the position. Kindly advise me in the matter at your earliest convenience.
Yours very truly,
R. M. COtJLTER,
Deputy Postmaster General.

This was written following an advice from the post office inspector recommending, not that the post office should be changed from Central Pai-k, but that the Post Office Department should act on his advice frequently tendered, and appoint a new postmaster. The answer to that was as follows:
New Westminster, June 24, 1910. Hon. E. Lemieux,
Postmaster General.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your 29755, I beg to recommend Mr. A. K. Farquharson as postmaster of Central Park. The district served by this office is rapidly filling up. and it has been urged that the office be moved to a more central location. I will take up this matter with the inspector, who will, no doubt, make recommendation regarding to same.
Yours faithfully,

As regards the importance of Central Park district, I might say that the department had received information from its own inspector that the district was growing rapidly, and he urged, therefore, that attention might be paid to his complaint. Here we have for the first time from this Mr. Robert Jardine, the. administrator of patronage for the Westminster district, the suggestion to the Postmaster General that he should close the office at Central Park, and remove it to another place. That was the origin of the closing of that post office which had been established for fourteen years. That suggestion was interpreted by the department, in the answer made by the hon. minister as:
Representations made to the department that by changing the location of the post office and establishing a post office at Colling-wood east, the interests of the majority of the residents would be best served.
Following this, and without the people interested having been given any information on the subject at all, when they went to their post office at Central Park, one Saturday evening, they found a written notice along side the delivery wicket as follows:
This post office will be closed to-night. After to-night you will get your mail at Keefer's.
Yet the Postmaster General told us that the Central Park post office was not closed, but that the post office had been merely removed to Keefer's. I would like to tell the hon. gentleman where Keefer's is, as he should know what is being done in his name in that district. Nearly all the people at Central Park have to make their living in Vancouver, which is six miles away, and in going to Vancouver they pass the Central Park post office every day. Keefer's is one mile further away from Vancouver than is Central Park, and none of the residents of Central Park have occasion to go to Keefer's in the ordinary course, and they would never go there unless compelled by the department. From Vancouver the settlement extends out Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
six miles to Central Park, and there is a post office at every mile on the way out. The Central Park office is the pioneer of them all, and is one mile from Collingwood East.
You say that post offices are established between Central Park and the city of Vancouver.

Yes, at Grand View, Cedar Cottage, Britcola, and Collingwood East. Then comes Central Park, the oldest and most thickly settled place, and the pioneer of them all, and the post office there was arbitrarily closed. Some 312 persons who used to get their mails there regularly were deprived of that advantage, and they petitioned the department, asking the Postmaster General to give his attention to the matter. As evidence that the public were not being served by the change, the people of Central Park got up a large public meeting, the largest ever held there. They first telegraphed the minister as follows :
Vancouver, British Columbia,
August 2, 1909.
Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Large public meeting at Central Park tonight protest against removal of post office to Keefer's. Resolution and petition following. MAXWELL SMITH.

Committee.
I may say that I attended that meeting by invitation, and that meeting was the largest ever held in that district. A resolution was there carried unanimously as follows:
That this public meeting of tbe residents and ratepayers of the Central Park district duly called and assembled this 2nd day of August, 1909, do hereby endorse tbe petition to the Postmaster General just read, protesting against the removal of the Central Park post office to Keefer's or any other point more than 500 yards from the present Central Park station. And be it further resolved that a copy of this resolution be forwarded along with the petition to the Postmaster General; and be it further resolved that a telegram be sent to-night to the Postmaster General advising him of this action; and be it further resolved that copies of this resolution and the heading of the petition be forwarded to the local post office inspector and local members of parliament.
I would like to read the letter which 1 addressed the Postmaster General at that time:
New Westminster, British Columbia.
August 9, 1909.
The Honourable the Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-As member for this district I have been requested to address you in connection with the closing of the post office at Central Park and the opening in its stead of an office at Keefer's, more than a mile distant from the late office, which was central to the population to be served. I have expressed to

these people at their public meeting my confidence that the facts of the case could not have been before the department when the order for the closing of the post office at Central Park was issued, and I trust your action on the petition now before you will bear out this view.
Offices are needed at Keefer's and at East Collingwood as well as at Central Park; but so long as there is only one office authorized Central Park is the natural place for it.
Faithfully yours,

Mr. Cowan also communicated with the Postmaster General as follows:
Vancouver, August 4, 1909. The Hon. Eodolphe Lemieux,
Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Sir,-A committee appointed bv the residents and ratepayers of Central Park to protest against the removal of the post office from that point, have asked me to communicate you my views on the subject.
This settlement is centrally located between the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster, on the interurban tram line. It was one of the first, if not the very first, settlements between the two cities, and is growing very rapidly. Many of its residents have located in business and established their homes there, just because of such public conveniences as the post office. Owing to the contour of the country and the present direction and state of the public roads, the removal of the office from Central Park to Keefer's must result in rendering it practically useless to the Central Park residents, and for the present, at least, of service to a much smaller number of the public. At any rate, whatever the public needs at Keefer's, they would seem to me to be such at Central Park, as without a doubt require retention of the post office at that point.
I am taking the liberty of writing you because I am confident that vou will look into the circumstances and do what is in the publio interest in the premises.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

I am sorry I weary the minister. But I assure him that the people affected by his action have been made a great deal more tired than he can possibly be made by this recital. Backing up these protests by the public meeting and the two parliamentary representatives of the district, there was forwarded a petition to the minister, bearing the names of 312 persons affected. Before this item is carried, I wish to say a few words as to the post office service in the province of Prince Edward Island, and especially in my own riding. Let me say that I have no specific fault to find with the administration of postal matters, but I wish respectfully to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the necessity for increased mail services. As we all know the statistics show that the province of Prince Edward Island is settled ten times more densely than any other province in Canada; in fact, the whole province is entirely settled, and as times goes by, the people feel the necessity for this increased accommodation. I am glad to say the Postmaster General is granting this accommodation, but perhaps not so rapidly as to satisfy the people. We have now a great number of free rural mail delivery routes and we ought to have in a very short time a complete System of rural mail delivery. But the principal thing I wish to urge is that in some places, perhaps not more than five or six miles removed from a railroad or a central point, which have only tri-weekly or semi-weekly mail delivery, a daily service should be oiven. I have received many petitions on

this subject, and I am sure that the department has received many asking for a daily delivery.
